cards.question: In one phrase, what does an operating system do?
cards.answer: Abstracts and arbitrates the underlying hardware.
distractors: Compiles and links the underlying applications.
Replaces the hardware with faster software.
Stores and backs up user files.

cards.question: What does "abstract" mean in the context of an OS?
cards.answer: Simplify what the hardware looks like to applications.
distractors: Decide which app gets which hardware resource.
Expose every hardware detail directly to applications.
Speed up the hardware with caching.

cards.question: What does "arbitrate" mean in the context of an OS?
cards.answer: Manage/control access to shared hardware.
distractors: Simplify what the hardware looks like to applications.
Translate source code into machine code.
Hide all hardware from the kernel.

cards.question: In the toy-shop analogy for an OS, what 3 things does the manager do?
cards.answer: Directs resources, enforces policies, mitigates complexity.
distractors: Writes code, compiles it, and ships it.
Buys hardware, builds toys, and ships orders.
Hires workers, trains them, and pays them.

cards.question: Which OS abstraction hides storage-device complexity (sectors/blocks)?
cards.answer: The file abstraction (read/write ops).
distractors: The socket abstraction (send/receive ops).
The page abstraction (map/swap ops).
The thread abstraction (fork/join ops).

cards.question: Which OS abstraction hides networking complexity (bits/packets)?
cards.answer: The socket abstraction (send/receive ops).
distractors: The file abstraction (read/write ops).
The page abstraction (map/swap ops).
The process abstraction (fork/exec ops).

cards.question: Why must an OS isolate applications from each other, even on old "single-app" devices like early phones?
cards.answer: Multiple apps still co-run and must not corrupt/read each other's data.
distractors: Early phones had too little memory to share.
Isolation is only needed on servers, not phones.
It's required only when apps are written in different languages.

cards.question: How does an OS enforce memory isolation between applications?
cards.answer: Allocates separate physical memory regions per app; blocks unintended cross-app access.
distractors: Lets apps share one memory region but checks each write afterward.
Gives each app its own CPU core.
Encrypts each app's data with a different key.

cards.question: Why is the file system considered part of the OS?
cards.answer: Hides storage hardware behind the file abstraction.
distractors: It's the program users use to edit files.
It's part of the hardware disk controller.
It's needed to compile programs.

cards.question: Why is a device driver considered part of the OS?
cards.answer: Manages a specific hardware device on the OS's behalf.
distractors: It's a user app that talks to the network.
It's part of the CPU's microcode.
It's the program that boots the computer.

cards.question: Why is the scheduler considered part of the OS?
cards.answer: Distributes CPU access among applications.
distractors: Decides which pages to evict from memory.
Translates virtual addresses to physical ones.
Manages the disk block layout.

cards.question: Is cache memory managed by the OS?
cards.answer: No — hardware manages the cache itself, even though the OS and apps benefit from it.
distractors: Yes, the OS decides which lines go in the cache.
Yes, apps must ask the OS before using the cache.
No, the compiler manages the cache.

cards.question: Why are a file editor and web browser NOT part of the OS?
cards.answer: They're user-facing apps that don't directly manage hardware.
distractors: They run in kernel mode but are optional.
They're part of the hardware firmware.
They manage the CPU on the user's behalf.

cards.question: Is distributing memory between processes an OS abstraction or arbitration?
cards.answer: Arbitration.
distractors: Abstraction.
Neither, it's a policy only.
Both equally.

cards.question: Is letting apps use different speakers/disks interchangeably an OS abstraction or arbitration?
cards.answer: Abstraction — same interface regardless of underlying hardware.
distractors: Arbitration: the OS decides which device each app gets.
Neither, the device driver handles it alone.
Arbitration: the OS splits speaker time between apps.

cards.question: What 3 core elements does an OS use to manage any resource (e.g. memory)?
cards.answer: Abstraction, mechanism, policy.
distractors: Process, thread, file.
Kernel, driver, application.
Hardware, firmware, software.

cards.question: For OS memory management, what "abstraction" represents a chunk of memory?
cards.answer: A memory page — a fixed-size addressable region (e.g. 4KB).
distractors: A memory segment of variable size.
A cache line (e.g., 64 B).
A physical DRAM chip.

cards.question: For OS memory management, what "mechanisms" operate on a memory page?
cards.answer: Allocate it in DRAM, map it into a process's address space, move/swap it.
distractors: Evict it using LRU.
Compile it and link it.
Encrypt it and checksum it.

cards.question: For OS memory management, what "policy" decides which pages to evict from RAM?
cards.answer: e.g. LRU (least recently used).
distractors: e.g., FIFO (first in, first out) of processes.
e.g., round robin.
e.g., copy-on-write.

cards.question: Which OS design principle says "build flexible mechanisms, not one hardcoded policy"?
cards.answer: Separation of mechanism and policy.
distractors: Optimize for the common case.
Separation of user and kernel mode.
Least privilege.

cards.question: Give an example of "separation of mechanism and policy" in memory management.
cards.answer: One page-access-tracking mechanism supports LRU, LFU, or random eviction policies.
distractors: A fixed LRU eviction policy built into the hardware.
Using separate page tables per process.
Swapping only when memory is completely full.

cards.question: Which OS design principle says "design based on actual expected hardware/workload"?
cards.answer: Optimize for the common case.
distractors: Separation of mechanism and policy.
Least privilege.
End-to-end argument.

cards.question: What are the 2 CPU privilege modes an OS relies on?
cards.answer: Kernel (privileged) mode and user (unprivileged) mode.
distractors: Root mode and guest mode.
Read mode and write mode.
Fast mode and safe mode.

cards.question: Which privilege mode does the OS kernel run in, and why?
cards.answer: Kernel mode — only it may directly access hardware.
distractors: User mode, so a bug can't crash the system.
Both modes equally, switching every timeslice.
User mode, because only apps touch hardware.

cards.question: What happens when a user-mode app attempts a privileged operation?
cards.answer: Hardware triggers a trap → control switches to the OS, which grants access or terminates the process.
distractors: The instruction runs normally, but slower.
The CPU reboots to protect itself.
The app is silently given kernel privileges.

cards.question: What is a system call?
cards.answer: An app's explicit request to the OS's exported interface for a privileged service.
distractors: A hardware interrupt raised by a device.
A function call inside the same user library.
A message the OS sends to an app.

cards.question: Name 3 example system calls and what each is for.
cards.answer: open (file access), send (socket access), malloc (memory allocation).
distractors: fork (file access), exec (socket access), kill (memory allocation).
read (socket access), mmap (file access), send (memory allocation).
open (memory allocation), send (file access), malloc (socket access).

cards.question: What are the basic steps of making a system call?
cards.answer: App writes args to a fixed location → invokes by call number → context switches to kernel → OS performs the op → switches back with results.
distractors: App jumps directly into kernel code → OS runs → app continues in kernel mode.
OS polls the app → copies args → runs the op in user mode.
App sends a signal → kernel forks a helper → helper returns results.

cards.question: Why are user/kernel mode transitions considered "expensive"?
cards.answer: ~50–100ns real overhead (2GHz Linux) + they evict app data from CPU cache.
distractors: They require a full reboot of the CPU pipeline (~10 ms).
They copy the whole address space each time.
They're not expensive; they cost about one instruction.

cards.question: In OS terms, what is a "signal"?
cards.answer: A mechanism for the OS to push notifications into an application.
distractors: A hardware wire that carries interrupts.
An app's request for a privileged service.
A lock used to synchronize threads.

cards.question: On 64-bit Linux, which system call sends a signal to a process?
cards.answer: kill
distractors: signal
send
term

cards.question: On 64-bit Linux, which system call sets a process's group ID?
cards.answer: setgid
distractors: setuid
chgrp
setpgid

cards.question: On 64-bit Linux, which system call mounts a file system?
cards.answer: mount
distractors: attach
fsopen
mkfs

cards.question: On 64-bit Linux, which system call reads/writes kernel system parameters?
cards.answer: sysctl
distractors: ioctl
sysconf
prctl

cards.question: What is a monolithic OS design?
cards.answer: Every possible service (all file systems, drivers, etc.) built directly into the kernel.
distractors: Only address spaces and threads in the kernel; everything else at user level.
A core kernel plus loadable modules.
An OS that runs a single application at a time.

cards.question: What's the main benefit of a monolithic OS design?
cards.answer: Everything bundled together enables compile-time optimizations.
distractors: Small size makes it easy to verify.
Modules can be swapped at runtime.
Few user/kernel crossings for IPC.

cards.question: What's the main downside of a monolithic OS design?
cards.answer: Huge codebase — hard to maintain; large memory footprint hurts performance.
distractors: Frequent costly user/kernel crossings for IPC.
Interface indirection limits optimizations.
Cannot run more than one application.

cards.question: What is a modular OS design (e.g. Linux)?
cards.answer: Core services + defined interfaces let functionality (file systems, schedulers) be added/swapped as modules.
distractors: Every service built directly into one kernel image.
Only IPC and threads in the kernel; services run at user level.
Each app ships its own copy of the kernel.

cards.question: What's the main benefit of a modular OS design?
cards.answer: Easier to maintain/upgrade; smaller, less resource-intensive.
distractors: Whole-kernel compile-time optimizations.
Easiest to formally verify.
No user/kernel crossings at all.

cards.question: What's the main downside of a modular OS design?
cards.answer: Interface layer limits some optimizations; disparate module code still causes bugs.
distractors: Huge memory footprint from bundling everything.
Frequent user/kernel crossings for IPC.
Cannot load new drivers without rewriting the kernel.

cards.question: What is a microkernel OS design?
cards.answer: Only bare primitives (address spaces, threads) stay in the kernel; everything else runs as user-level processes via IPC.
distractors: Core kernel plus loadable modules for file systems and drivers.
Every service built into one kernel image.
A kernel that runs entirely in user mode.

cards.question: What's the main benefit of a microkernel design?
cards.answer: Small size → low overhead, easy to verify/test (good for embedded/control systems).
distractors: Compile-time optimizations across all services.
Loadable modules for any workload.
Very high portability across hardware.

cards.question: What's the main downside of a microkernel design?
cards.answer: Poor portability, added complexity, frequent costly user/kernel crossings from heavy IPC.
distractors: Huge code base that's hard to maintain.
Interface layer limits some optimizations.
Can't isolate faulty drivers from the kernel.

cards.question: In the Linux OS architecture, what are the layers from hardware up to applications?
cards.answer: Hardware → kernel → standard libraries (syscall interfaces) → utility programs → user apps.
distractors: Hardware → user apps → standard libraries → kernel.
Hardware → utility programs → kernel → user apps.
Kernel → hardware → standard libraries → user apps.

cards.question: What's at the core of the Mac OS X architecture?
cards.answer: The Mach microkernel (memory mgmt, thread scheduling, IPC/RPC).
distractors: A monolithic Linux kernel.
The BSD kernel with loadable modules.
The Windows NT kernel.

cards.question: What does the BSD layer add on top of Mac OS X's Mach microkernel?
cards.answer: Unix interoperability — BSD CLI, POSIX API, network I/O.
distractors: Memory management and thread scheduling.
The graphical user interface.
Device driver development kits only.

cards.question: Name 2 desktop/server OS families.
cards.answer: Microsoft Windows, and UNIX-based (Linux, Mac OS X).
cards.memory: UNIX was born at Bell Labs in the late 1960s.
distractors: Android and iOS.
Symbian and Mach.
BSD and Zygote.

cards.question: Which UNIX variant does Mac OS X extend?
cards.answer: BSD (Berkeley Software Distribution).
distractors: System V.
Linux.
Minix.

cards.question: Name 2 embedded/mobile OSes.
cards.answer: Android (embedded Linux) and iOS.
cards.memory: Android versions have dessert names: KitKat, Ice Cream Sandwich.
distractors: Windows and Mac OS X.
Linux and BSD.
Mach and Solaris.

cards.question: Which OS does this course use for most examples?
cards.answer: Linux
distractors: Windows
Mac OS X
Solaris

cards.question: Give an example of an OS resource-limit policy.
cards.answer: A maximum number of open files (or sockets) per process.
cards.memory: Policy = a rule, often a limit.
distractors: Evicting the least recently used page.
Mapping a page into an address space.
Using a file abstraction for disks.

cards.question: What does the OS do with memory pages it rarely uses?
cards.answer: Swaps them to disk to free up DRAM.
cards.memory: Swap = move the dusty box to the garage.
distractors: Deletes them permanently.
Compresses them into the CPU cache.
Copies them to every other process.

cards.question: Which OS service manages CPU access?
cards.answer: The scheduler.
cards.memory: One OS service per piece of hardware.
distractors: The memory manager.
The block device driver.
The file system.

cards.question: Which OS service manages physical memory?
cards.answer: The memory manager.
cards.memory: It also keeps apps out of each other's memory.
distractors: The scheduler.
The block device driver.
The file system.

cards.question: Which OS service manages disk access?
cards.answer: The block device driver.
distractors: The scheduler.
The memory manager.
The socket layer.

cards.question: Name a higher-level OS service not tied to one device.
cards.answer: The file system (the file abstraction).
cards.memory: File = an idea built on top of disks.
distractors: The block device driver.
The scheduler.
The memory manager.

cards.question: How are system-call arguments passed to the kernel?
cards.answer: Directly, or indirectly by passing their address.
distractors: Only through CPU registers, never by address.
By sending them as signals.
The kernel reads them directly from the app's source code.

cards.question: By default, does a process wait for its system call to finish?
cards.answer: Yes. Syscalls are synchronous by default.
cards.memory: Asynchronous syscalls come later in the course.
distractors: No. Syscalls are always asynchronous.
Only if the syscall touches the disk.
No. The process keeps running in kernel mode.

cards.question: What does the syscall return path involve?
cards.answer: Switch back to user mode, copy results, jump to right after the call.
cards.memory: Return = undo every step of the entry.
distractors: Stay in kernel mode and jump to the app's main function.
Restart the process from its first instruction.
Copy the kernel's stack into the app.

cards.question: Are Windows and UNIX syscall sets very different?
cards.answer: No. Both offer similar process, file, and device calls.
distractors: Yes. They share no common abstractions.
Yes. Windows has no process or file calls.
No. They use identical system call numbers.

cards.question: Where does the CPU know it's in kernel mode?
cards.answer: A special privilege bit in the CPU is set.
cards.memory: Bit on = kernel; bit off = user.
distractors: The stack pointer points into kernel memory.
The program counter is set to zero.
A flag in the process's PCB is set.
